summary: For predicate-felony sequencing, the relevant date is the original sentence date on the prior conviction, not a later resentencing date after an illegal sentence is corrected. Resentencing did not reset sequentiality under Penal Law 70.06.

Defendant impliedly consented to monitoring and recording of his nonprivileged jail calls, so admission of call excerpts did not violate state or federal wiretap law or the state right to counsel. Remaining claims were either unpreserved or meritless.

A pretrial detainee notified that calls are monitored and recorded has no objectively reasonable Fourth Amendment privacy expectation in those calls. Jail officials may share such recordings with prosecutors without a warrant.
Photographs were sufficiently authenticated through complainant and law-enforcement extraction testimony. Admission of the photographs was within the trial court's discretion.

Coram nobis relief was properly denied because defendant failed to show ineffective assistance of appellate counsel under New York's meaningful-representation standard. Claimed failures in issue selection, briefing quality, and communication did not establish deprivation of fair process.

Assuming error in admitting a custodial statement under pedigree/Miranda rules, any error was harmless given overwhelming proof that defendant possessed the drugs and paraphernalia in the bedroom where he was found. Conviction affirmed.

A witness's prior grand-jury testimony was properly admitted as past recollection recorded after a sufficient foundation. Because the declarant testified and was subject to cross-examination, there was no Confrontation Clause violation.

County Court properly found defendant violated his cooperation agreement by refusing to testify in a related prosecution after agreeing to cooperate completely and truthfully. Denial of plea withdrawal and ineffective-assistance claims were upheld.

Conviction was affirmed, but Supreme Court abused its discretion by summarily denying defendant's CPL 440.10 conflict-of-interest motion without a hearing. Case was modified to require a hearing on that postconviction claim.
Police encounter escalated beyond a level-one request for information, and the People failed to preserve any alternative De Bour justification. Suppression was granted and the indictment dismissed.

Trial judge's personal quid-pro-quo cooperation deal with a codefendant witness created an unconstitutional appearance and risk of bias by assuming an advocacy role. Error required reversal and a new trial before a different judge.

No reasonable view of the evidence supported a deadly-force justification instruction where defendant struck complainant in the head with a pint glass after only a push. Denial of the requested justification charge was proper.

Defendant was the initial deadly-force aggressor as a matter of law when he drew his gun during a nondeadly confrontation, so he was not entitled to a justification charge. Appellate Division reversal was itself reversed.

Under these facts, conviction for second-degree assault by dangerous instrument necessarily involved deadly physical force, so the trial court's justification instructions were proper. Other claims were unpreserved or without merit.

A reconstruction hearing was proper to determine whether a disputed exhibit was actually a jury note triggering CPL 310.30 duties. Record supported the finding that it was a discarded draft note, so no O'Rama/Parker error occurred.

For a missing-witness charge, the proponent need not initially negate cumulativeness; that burden is on the opponent once prima facie entitlement is shown. Denial of the charge here was error and not harmless, requiring a new trial.

Accusatory allegations were sufficient to support an inference that defendant was the vehicle operator involved in the accident. Appellate Term's dismissal on that ground was reversed and the case remitted for unresolved issues.

Trial court did not abuse discretion in denying self-representation where defendant was found to be malingering and likely to disrupt proceedings. Reasonable-suspicion determination had record support and was beyond further review.

Even assuming suppression of impeachment material and imperfect correction of witness testimony, there was no reasonable possibility of a different verdict under New York's Brady materiality standard. CPL 440 relief was properly denied.
Counsel's jury-nullification-themed defense did not, on the total record, constitute ineffective assistance. Conviction was affirmed.
On direct appeal, the record did not conclusively establish ineffective assistance concerning surveillance-video strategy. Any DNA confrontation error was harmless, so conviction was affirmed.

The People violated Brady by failing to disclose surveillance video from the shooting scene that had impeachment/exculpatory value. There was a reasonable probability of a different result, requiring reversal and a new trial.
Batson challenge was properly rejected based on a supported race-neutral explanation, and consecutive sentencing for weapon possession and murder was lawful under Brown. Conviction was affirmed.

A Facebook account itself is not an "internet identifier" under Correction Law's definition, so indictment for failing to register it did not charge a crime. Conviction was reversed and the indictment dismissed.

Trial court properly denied a third-degree-assault lesser-included charge because any such verdict would have been speculative on this record. Assuming admission of the 911 call was error, it was harmless.

Assuming error in refusing second-degree manslaughter and criminally negligent homicide as remote lessers, the error was harmless where the jury convicted on the highest submitted homicide count despite an available intermediate lesser.
On this record there was no basis to disturb suppression, and the Appellate Division did not violate LaFontaine/Nicholson limits. Order affirmed.
No reasonable view of the evidence supported anything less than serious physical injury from the attack, so defendant was not entitled to a third-degree-assault lesser charge. Conviction affirmed.

A defendant held for grand-jury action on a class A felony punishable by life could not validly waive indictment and plead by SCI to a lesser offense. Plea was vacated, SCI dismissed, and felony complaint reinstated.

By refusing to provide meaningful defense access to favorable witnesses or workable contact means, the People suppressed Brady material. Under New York's specific-request standard, materiality was shown and a new trial was ordered.

A juror's extensive texting, media access, concealment, false sworn statements, and evidence destruction constituted egregious misconduct that may have affected a substantial right. Verdict was set aside and a new trial ordered.

Grand-jury proof was insufficient that defendant came dangerously near stealing property above felony-value thresholds, so attempted grand-larceny counts were unsupported. Appellate Division was modified to restore dismissal/reduction entered below.

People's appeal was dismissed sua sponte for lack of Court of Appeals jurisdiction because the Appellate Division's modification rested on an unpreserved issue, i.e., an interest-of-justice determination rather than a reviewable question of law.

Constitutional challenge to Executive Law 552 was unpreserved and Appellate Division's refusal to reach it in the interest of justice was not reviewable. Voluntariness suppression claim was a mixed question with record support.

Evidence was legally sufficient to infer defendant orchestrated a forged-check scheme by opening an account, enabling deposit, and rapidly withdrawing funds in structured transactions. Grand-larceny conviction was affirmed.

A guilty plea does not waive a jurisdictional challenge to the count of conviction even when another lower-grade count in the same complaint is facially sufficient. Reversal of the conviction on the defective top count was affirmed.

CPL 520.30 authorizes courts to scrutinize the adequacy and public-policy sufficiency of collateral backing an insurance-company bail bond; deference to insurer business judgment is not required. Disapproval of the bond and denial of habeas relief were reinstated.

Trial court committed reversible error by barring cross-examination of key police witnesses on specific dishonesty matters, including prior judicial credibility findings and misleading statements to a prosecutor. New trial ordered.

A physician's reckless prescribing practices in a "pill mill" can support homicide liability where statutory manslaughter elements, including recklessness and causation, are proved. Manslaughter convictions for two patient overdose deaths were upheld.

Appeal-waiver analysis in consolidated cases: waiver was valid in Thomas, but invalid in Green and Lang because misleading colloquies mischaracterized waiver scope and voluntariness. Resulting orders were affirmed in Thomas and reversed in Green/Lang.

Defendant's only argument on appeal, challenging standing to contest a search after marshal possession of the apartment, was unpreserved and no preservation exception applied. No reviewable question of law was presented.
Both trial courts erred by changing charge rulings after summations, but each error was harmless under the circumstances. Convictions in both consolidated appeals were affirmed.

Denial of a for-cause challenge was within discretion because voir dire responses, viewed in context, did not show disqualifying bias requiring further rehabilitation. Suppression and legal-sufficiency claims were also rejected.

Accusatory instrument for second-degree criminal contempt was facially sufficient to infer intent to violate a stay-away order, and plea allocution was adequate on this record. Conviction was affirmed.
A suppression court has discretion to reopen a hearing after the People rest but before the court renders a decision, and no abuse occurred here. Suppression denial and conviction were affirmed.

Evidence was legally sufficient to prove intent to defraud in first-degree forged-instrument possession based on circumstances including quantity, separation of counterfeit from genuine bills, and context. Expert-testimony objections were unpreserved, and stop-related suppression was properly denied.

Prison-clothing fair-trial claim was unpreserved; denial of a for-cause juror challenge was proper; and any error admitting defendant's videotaped statement was harmless in light of overwhelming evidence. Conviction affirmed.
